short: Britain's tank crews stopped being a machine-gun detachment and became a corps.
full:
The men who took the first tanks into action belonged to the Heavy Section, Machine Gun Corps, a cover name settled in 1916 that concealed what they drove and left them administratively attached to somebody else's weapon. Eight companies were expanded into battalions in November that year and the force was renamed the Heavy Branch. Its headquarters and depot went to Bovington in Dorset, which has been the home of British armour ever since.

A Royal Warrant separated the Heavy Branch from the Machine Gun Corps and constituted it as the Tank Corps on 28 July 1917, four months before Cambrai. Hugh Elles commanded it, with J. F. C. Fuller as his chief staff officer, and the corps at last controlled its own recruiting, training and doctrine rather than arguing for machines through other people's channels. It became the Royal Tank Corps in 1923 and the Royal Tank Regiment in 1939, keeping the brown, red and green colours and the motto Fear Naught.
